chunks.text: At half past nine on Tuesday, 2 June 1891, Constable Dyer found Josiah Pemberton, master clockmaker of Clerkenwell, unconscious on his workshop floor. His regulator clock lay smashed beside him, and the working sheet of his new detent escapement - the work of five years - was gone. Four people had business with the shop that day. Every one of them tells the truth, in a manner of speaking. Separate what each person literally says from what they want you to believe, and combine the documents to find who was in the workshop.
chunks.title: Case introduction: The Clockmaker's Secret

chunks.text: WORKSHOP DIARY of Josiah Pemberton. 12 Feb. - Had a second key cut for Mary, who grumbles at waiting on the step in the cold of a morning. Told her to guard it well. 28 May. - Mary asked again after the lift angle of my new detent escapement. Told her the figure lives in my head and nowhere else. 2 June, 5:30 PM.
chunks.title: Workshop Diary
chunks.author: Josiah Pemberton

chunks.text: 2 June, 5:30 PM. - Stone called at the counter, offering money. Refused him. 2 June, 6:30 PM. - Oliver gone home. 2 June, 7:05 PM. - Mary asked once more, as she was leaving, whether I would let her see the angle. Refused her again; she went without a word. Locked the shop after her. I shall work on the Harcourt carriage clock until ten.
chunks.title: Workshop Diary
chunks.author: Josiah Pemberton

chunks.text:
Frederick Stone, Clockmaker, to Josiah Pemberton.

Dear Pemberton, I have heard of your detent escapement and the remarkable accuracy it promises. I will give you five hundred pounds for the design, complete. I understand that the critical figure, the lift angle, has been entrusted to no one. Would you reconsider? I remain at your service, F. Stone.
chunks.title: Technical Letter from Mr. Stone
chunks.author: Frederick Stone

chunks.text:
Inspection of the workshop by Inspector Gregson.

The workshop regulator clock was found on the floor beside Mr. Pemberton, its glass broken and the movement stopped at 8:47 PM. A regulator that falls from its wall stops at the moment it is struck. The back door and the shop door were locked from outside; neither was forced. The shop door lock is intact. The workshop has two keys: the master's and the one cut in February.
chunks.title: Workshop Clock Inspection Report
chunks.author: Inspector Gregson

chunks.text:
Torn lower half of a sheet found beneath Mr. Pemberton's hand.

"Detent escapement, version 4. Pallet lift: ____ degrees (to be entered when trials are done). Note: M. asked after the lift angle again tonight. Told her nothing; written nowhere. I do not like how she looks at the drawers. Do not trust - "
(The remainder is torn away.)
chunks.title: Partially Completed Design Note
chunks.author: Josiah Pemberton

chunks.text:
Statement of Oliver Grant.

I left at half past six, as the diary will confirm, and went straight home to my lodgings in Bethnal Green. My landlady will tell you I was in by eight and did not go out again.
chunks.title: Statement of Mr. Oliver Grant
chunks.author: Oliver Grant

chunks.text:
Statement of Frederick Stone.

I have not been inside Pemberton's workshop in over a year. I spent Tuesday evening at the Horological Society dinner in Clerkenwell Road, which began at seven and ended after ten. I did call at the shop at half past five and was refused.
chunks.title: Statement of Mr. Frederick Stone
chunks.author: Frederick Stone

chunks.text:
Statement of Mary Collins.

I locked the shop at seven o'clock and handed Mr. Pemberton his key, as I always do. After that I never touched his key again. The next I knew of the matter was when Constable Dyer called at my lodgings in Islington at ten.
chunks.title: Statement of Miss Mary Collins
chunks.author: Mary Collins

chunks.text:
Statement of Captain Arthur Finch.

I collected my chronometer at ten past six and left. I never set foot in the workshop that day. At twenty past eight I returned to the shop door because the chronometer was losing. Mr. Pemberton spoke to me through the door. He said he could not attend me, as he was engaged with someone over the very matter he had refused an hour ago. I heard a woman's voice behind him.
chunks.title: Statement of Captain Arthur Finch
chunks.author: Arthur Finch

chunks.text: Oliver Grant, Pemberton's apprentice. Background: An eager apprentice in his third year who idolises his master. Quick-tempered and proud of his craft. Motive: Pemberton refused to let him work on the new escapement, calling him too young. Relationship: Apprentice of Josiah Pemberton. Known whereabouts: Left at half past six; at his lodgings in Bethnal Green from eight.
chunks.title: Profile of Oliver Grant

chunks.text: Personality: Earnest, indignant at suspicion, answers literally. He left at half past six and went straight home, where his landlady saw him in by eight. He did not go out again. He knows nothing of the key arrangement. Does not know: That Mary had a second key.
chunks.title: Private knowledge of Oliver Grant

chunks.text: Questions: Where were you at eight? Where were you that evening? When did you leave? Answer: I left at half past six, as the diary says, and went straight home to Bethnal Green. My landlady saw me in by eight and I did not go out again.
chunks.title: Oliver Grant on: Where were you at eight

chunks.text: Questions: Who has keys to the workshop? Who had a key? Did anyone have a second key? Answer: Mr. Pemberton had the key. Mary closed up each evening and handed it to him. I never had one, and I know of no second.
chunks.title: Oliver Grant on: Who has keys to the workshop

chunks.text: Questions: Why were you refused the escapement? Did you want the design? Do you have a motive? Answer: He said I was too young. I was cross, but I would not steal what I hope one day to be taught.
chunks.title: Oliver Grant on: Why were you refused the escapement

chunks.text: Questions: Who do you suspect? What about Mary, Mr. Stone or Mr. Finch? Answer: Mr. Stone wanted the design badly, everyone knew it. And Mr. Finch came knocking late. I will not say more.
chunks.title: Oliver Grant on: Who do you suspect

chunks.text: Frederick Stone, a rival clockmaker. Background: Pemberton's long-time rival, jealous of his reputation. Polished, silky, and a master of phrasing. Motive: Offered five hundred pounds for the escapement, and was refused. His own business is failing. Relationship: Rival of Josiah Pemberton. Known whereabouts: Called at the shop at half past five; then at the Horological Society dinner from seven until after ten.
chunks.title: Profile of Frederick Stone

chunks.text: Personality: Smooth, careful, deliberately literal, avoids direct lies. He called at the shop front at half past five and was refused. He then went to the Horological Society dinner in Clerkenwell Road, which lasted from seven until after ten. He wrote the technical letter offering five hundred pounds. He has not been inside the workshop proper for a year, which is literally true, but he did visit the shop front. Does not know: Who entered the workshop that night.
chunks.title: Private knowledge of Frederick Stone

chunks.text: Questions: Have you been in the workshop? When were you last at Pemberton's? Did you visit the shop? Answer: I have not been inside Pemberton's workshop in over a year. I did call at the front of the shop on Tuesday at half past five, on business, and was refused.
chunks.title: Frederick Stone on: Have you been in the workshop

chunks.text: Questions: Where were you at eight? Where were you that evening? What about the dinner? Answer: I was at the Horological Society dinner in Clerkenwell Road, which began at seven and ended after ten. Fifty gentlemen can say so.
chunks.title: Frederick Stone on: Where were you at eight

chunks.text: Questions: Why did you write the letter offering money? Did you want the escapement? Do you have a motive? Answer: I made a business offer, as any prudent tradesman would. It was refused. I bear no grudge.
chunks.title: Frederick Stone on: Why did you write the letter offering money

chunks.text: Questions: Have you spoken to Mr. Pemberton? When did you last speak to him? Answer: I spoke to him at the counter at half past five on Tuesday, and wrote to him on Friday. I have not spoken to him since.
chunks.title: Frederick Stone on: Have you spoken to Mr. Pemberton

chunks.text: Questions: Who do you suspect? What about Mary, Oliver or Arthur? Answer: Pemberton's assistant knew his habits better than any man. I say no more.
chunks.title: Frederick Stone on: Who do you suspect

chunks.text: Mary Collins, Pemberton's assistant. Background: Pemberton's assistant for nine years and a gifted clock-finisher, who has never been allowed to learn the new design. Quiet, controlled, with a widowed mother to support and rent arrears. Motive: Repeatedly refused the secret of the new escapement, which Mr. Stone would pay heavily for; her mother's rent is overdue. Relationship: Assistant to Josiah Pemberton. Known whereabouts: Claims to have left at seven and to have been home in Islington before ten.
chunks.title: Profile of Mary Collins

chunks.text: Personality: Composed, exact, chooses words with great care, never volunteers anything. SECRET (never admit): she left at seven, returned at about ten past eight with the second key Mr. Pemberton had cut for her in February, was refused again, struck him in the struggle at 8:47, and took the working sheet. Every sentence she speaks is carefully true or evasive. She never lies outright and never confesses. Does not know: That Mr. Finch spoke to Mr. Pemberton at the door at twenty past eight.
chunks.title: Private knowledge of Mary Collins

chunks.text: Questions: Do you have a key to the workshop? Who has keys to the workshop? Do you hold a key? Answer: I locked the shop at seven and handed Mr. Pemberton his key, as I always do. After that I never touched his key again.
chunks.title: Mary Collins on: Do you have a key to the workshop

chunks.text: Questions: Did you have a second key? Why does the diary say a second key was cut for you? Why did you not mention the other key? Answer: Mr. Pemberton once had a key cut so that I could open in the cold of a morning. I did not say I had no key. I said I never touched his.
chunks.title: Mary Collins on: Did you have a second key

chunks.text: Questions: Where were you at eight? Where were you that evening? When did you leave? Answer: I left at seven, and was home in Islington before ten. I do not keep a clock in my head for every minute between.
chunks.title: Mary Collins on: Where were you at eight

chunks.text: Questions: Did you see Mr. Pemberton after seven? Did you speak to him that evening? Did you ask about the escapement? Answer: The last I knew of the matter was when Constable Dyer called at my lodgings at ten. I asked about the escapement often, as any assistant might. He always said no.
chunks.title: Mary Collins on: Did you see Mr. Pemberton after seven

chunks.text: Questions: Why did Mr. Pemberton refuse you at seven? Who was refused an hour ago? Who did he refuse? Answer: I cannot say what Mr. Pemberton thought on any subject. He refused many people many things.
chunks.title: Mary Collins on: Why did Mr. Pemberton refuse you at seven

chunks.text: Questions: Do you need money? Do you have a motive? Why would you want the design? Answer: My mother's rent is overdue, I do not hide it. But the design is of no use to me; I cannot sell what I cannot complete.
chunks.title: Mary Collins on: Do you need money

chunks.text: Arthur Finch, a regular customer. Background: A retired naval officer who owns several costly chronometers. Courteous, exact, slightly deaf and fond of precise wording. Motive: None known beyond a long-standing admiration for Pemberton's work. Relationship: Regular customer of Pemberton & Son. Known whereabouts: Collected his chronometer at ten past six; returned briefly at twenty past eight.
chunks.title: Profile of Arthur Finch

chunks.text: Personality: Courteous, precise, careful about what he actually heard versus guessed. He collected his chronometer at ten past six and left. At twenty past eight he returned because the chronometer was losing, found the shop shut, knocked, and spoke through the shop door with Mr. Pemberton, who said he could not attend him: he was engaged with someone over the very matter he had refused an hour ago. Finch heard a woman's voice behind him. Does not know: Who the visitor was.
chunks.title: Private knowledge of Arthur Finch

chunks.text: Questions: When did you collect your chronometer? When were you at the shop? Did you go back? Answer: I collected it at ten past six and left. I never set foot in the workshop that day. I did go back to the shop front at twenty past eight, but the door was shut.
chunks.title: Arthur Finch on: When did you collect your chronometer

chunks.text: Questions: What did Mr. Pemberton say at twenty past eight? What did you hear? Who was with him? Answer: Through the shop door he told me he could not attend to me; he was engaged with someone over the very matter he had refused an hour ago. I heard a woman's voice behind him, but I could not say whose.
chunks.title: Arthur Finch on: What did Mr. Pemberton say at twenty past eight

chunks.text: Questions: Why did you not mention that earlier? Why did you say you did not set foot in the workshop? Answer: I did not set foot in the workshop, and said so. I stood at the shop door. You did not ask me what I heard.
chunks.title: Arthur Finch on: Why did you not mention that earlier

chunks.text: Questions: Who do you suspect? What about Mary, Oliver or Mr. Stone? Answer: I would not guess. I heard a woman's voice, that is all.
chunks.title: Arthur Finch on: Who do you suspect

chunks.text: Dr. Watson: "Mind the exact words, my friend. Several of our witnesses say nothing false, and yet leave an impression that is. Ask what each statement carefully avoids saying."
chunks.title: Watson hint 1

chunks.text: Dr. Watson: "Mr. Pemberton's diary records a key cut for someone. Compare the precise wording of the keyholder's statement. Whose key did she say she never touched?"
chunks.title: Watson hint 2

chunks.text: Dr. Watson: "Mr. Pemberton told Captain Finch he was engaged over a matter refused 'an hour ago', at twenty past eight. Whom did he refuse at about seven - and whom at half past five? Then note when the regulator stopped."
chunks.title: Watson hint 3
